theory.intro: Rectangles with the same area can have different side lengths, and rectangles with the same perimeter can also have different shapes.
facts: Area $=$ length $\times$ width; many length/width pairs give the **same area**.
Perimeter $=$ $2 \times (\text{length} + \text{width})$; many pairs give the **same perimeter**.
Same area does **not** mean same perimeter, and the reverse is also true.
For whole-number rectangles, use positive side lengths and count a turned rectangle only once.
For a known area, multiply the pair to check it. For a known perimeter, the two lengths add to half the perimeter.
steps: Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.
Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.
List the requested dimensions or compare the results.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) List all different rectangles with whole-number side lengths and area $56\text{ m}^2$, counting a turned rectangle only once.
(b) What is the connection to the factors of $56$?
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
List positive whole-number pairs with product $56$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$1\times56=56$.
$2\times28=56$.
$4\times14=56$.
$7\times8=56$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
(a) The dimensions are $1\text{ m}$ by $56\text{ m}$, $2\text{ m}$ by $28\text{ m}$, $4\text{ m}$ by $14\text{ m}$ and $7\text{ m}$ by $8\text{ m}$. (b) The possible side lengths are factor pairs of $56$.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) List all different rectangles with whole-number side lengths and perimeter $22\text{ cm}$, counting a turned rectangle only once.
(b) Calculate each area and identify the greatest.
workedExamples.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Half the perimeter is $22\div2=11\text{ cm}$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$1\text{ cm}$ by $10\text{ cm}$: $A=10\text{ cm}^2$
$2\text{ cm}$ by $9\text{ cm}$: $A=18\text{ cm}^2$
$3\text{ cm}$ by $8\text{ cm}$: $A=24\text{ cm}^2$
$4\text{ cm}$ by $7\text{ cm}$: $A=28\text{ cm}^2$
$5\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$: $A=30\text{ cm}^2$

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
(a) The five dimension pairs are listed above. (b) $5\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$ has the greatest area, $30\text{ cm}^2$.

**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Check both measures for each pair of rectangles.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
(a) $18\times5=90\text{ cm}^2$.
$15\times6=90\text{ cm}^2$.
$2\times(18+5)=46\text{ cm}$.
$2\times(15+6)=42\text{ cm}$.
$46-42=4\text{ cm}$.
(b) $2\times(23+4)=54\text{ m}$.
$2\times(16+11)=54\text{ m}$.
$23\times4=92\text{ m}^2$.
$16\times11=176\text{ m}^2$.
$176-92=84\text{ m}^2$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
(a) Both areas are $90\text{ cm}^2$, but the $15\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$ rectangle has perimeter $4\text{ cm}$ smaller. (b) Both perimeters are $54\text{ m}$, but the $16\text{ m}$ by $11\text{ m}$ rectangle has $84\text{ m}^2$ more area.

foundation.question_text:
A rectangle has area $24\text{ cm}^{2}$ and length $8$ cm.
Find its width.
foundation.solution_text:

The area is $24\text{ cm}^2$ and one side is $8\text{ cm}$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$24\div8=3\text{ cm}$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
The width is $3\text{ cm}$.

**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Check both areas are $24\text{ cm}^2$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$P_{12\times2}=2\times(12+2)=28\text{ cm}$.
$P_{6\times4}=2\times(6+4)=20\text{ cm}$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
The perimeters are $28\text{ cm}$ and $20\text{ cm}$.

**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Check both perimeters are $20\text{ cm}$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$8\times2=16\text{ cm}^2$.
$5\times5=25\text{ cm}^2$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
The areas are $16\text{ cm}^2$ and $25\text{ cm}^2$.

foundation.solution_text:

$2\times9=18$.
$3\times6=18$.

foundation.question_text:
List all different rectangles with whole-number side lengths and perimeter $16$ cm.
Treat a rotation as the same rectangle.
foundation.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Half the perimeter is $16\div2=8\text{ cm}$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$1\text{ cm}$ by $7\text{ cm}$
$2\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$
$3\text{ cm}$ by $5\text{ cm}$
$4\text{ cm}$ by $4\text{ cm}$

foundation.question_text:
Two rectangles have the same area.
Must they have the same perimeter?
Use the $3$ cm by $8$ cm and $4$ cm by $6$ cm rectangles to decide.
foundation.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Check the two products for area and compare their perimeters.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$3\times8=24\text{ cm}^2$.
$4\times6=24\text{ cm}^2$.
$2\times(3+8)=22\text{ cm}$.
$2\times(4+6)=20\text{ cm}$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
No. Both areas are $24\text{ cm}^2$, but their perimeters are $22\text{ cm}$ and $20\text{ cm}$.

development.question_text:
Complete the table of whole-number dimensions for rectangles of area $36\text{ m}^{2}$.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Length (m)}&\text{Width (m)}\\\hline1&36\\2&18\\3&12\\4&\square\\6&6\end{array}$
development.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
The missing width must multiply $4\text{ m}$ to give $36\text{ m}^2$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$36\div4=9\text{ m}$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
The missing table entry is $9\text{ m}$.

development.question_text:
Rectangles A and B both have area $48\text{ cm}^{2}$.
A is $12$ cm by $4$ cm.
B is $8$ cm long.
Find B's width, then decide which rectangle has the smaller perimeter.
development.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Use B's area and length to find its width first.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
B's width: $48\div8=6\text{ cm}$.
$P_A=2\times(12+4)=32\text{ cm}$.
$P_B=2\times(8+6)=28\text{ cm}$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
B has width $6\text{ cm}$ and the smaller perimeter, $28\text{ cm}$.

development.question_text: Two rectangular display boards each have perimeter $28$ m. One is $11$ m by $3$ m and the other is $8$ m by $6$ m. Compare their areas.
development.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Check both perimeters are $28\text{ m}$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$11\times3=33\text{ m}^2$.
$8\times6=48\text{ m}^2$.
$48-33=15\text{ m}^2$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
The $8\text{ m}$ by $6\text{ m}$ board has $15\text{ m}^2$ more area.

development.question_text:
All whole-number rectangles with perimeter $24$ cm have side lengths that add to $12$ cm.
List the possible dimension pairs and identify the one with the greatest area.
development.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Use each positive whole-number pair with sum $12$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$1\text{ cm}$ by $11\text{ cm}$: $A=11\text{ cm}^2$
$2\text{ cm}$ by $10\text{ cm}$: $A=20\text{ cm}^2$
$3\text{ cm}$ by $9\text{ cm}$: $A=27\text{ cm}^2$
$4\text{ cm}$ by $8\text{ cm}$: $A=32\text{ cm}^2$
$5\text{ cm}$ by $7\text{ cm}$: $A=35\text{ cm}^2$
$6\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$: $A=36\text{ cm}^2$

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
The $6\text{ cm}$ by $6\text{ cm}$ rectangle has greatest area $36\text{ cm}^2$.

development.question_text:
All whole-number rectangles with area $40\text{ cm}^{2}$ are listed by factor pairs.
Complete the list: $(1,40)$, $(2,20)$, $(4,10)$, $(\square,\square)$.
development.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
The missing pair must multiply to $40$.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$1\times40=40$.
$2\times20=40$.
$4\times10=40$.
$5\times8=40$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
The missing pair is $(5,8)$, giving a rectangle $5\text{ cm}$ by $8\text{ cm}$.

development.question_text:
A rectangle is changed from $10$ cm by $4$ cm to $8$ cm by $5$ cm.
Describe what stays the same and what changes.
development.solution_text:
**Use the area or perimeter to find or check the dimension pairs.**
Compare the area and perimeter before and after the change.

**Calculate any missing dimensions and the required area or perimeter.**
$10\times4=40\text{ cm}^2$.
$8\times5=40\text{ cm}^2$.
$2\times(10+4)=28\text{ cm}$.
$2\times(8+5)=26\text{ cm}$.
$28-26=2\text{ cm}$.

**List the requested dimensions or compare the results.**
The area stays $40\text{ cm}^2$; the perimeter decreases by $2\text{ cm}$.
